strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant gap: direct feed-forward multi-view reconstruction for fisheye and equirectangular imagery, where pinhole-oriented foundation models can fail severely.

The integration of a permutation-equivariant multi-view backbone with angular/radial ray prediction and camera-type conditioning is sensible. Although the ingredients draw heavily from π3, UniK3D, and calibration-token work, applying them jointly to wide-FoV multi-view geometry is a useful contribution.

The experimental scope is broad, covering pose estimation, point-map reconstruction, large-scale localization, and monocular panoramic depth across fisheye and 360-degree datasets. Reported improvements over VGGT and π3 are often very large; for example, Stanford2D3D AUC@30 increases from roughly 2 to 79.93, and reconstruction metrics improve substantially across all three evaluated datasets.

The method offers a compelling efficiency advantage over SfM-based 360-degree localization: approximately 3 seconds versus minutes in the Matterport3D comparison, while registering every view in the three tested scenes. Qualitative results also suggest substantially more complete reconstructions.

The ablations provide some evidence that camera tokens, mixed-camera training, and larger multi-view batches are beneficial, and the paper clearly acknowledges the limited availability of labeled 360-degree training data.
weaknesses: The central comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed architecture from training and data advantages. Wid3R initializes from π3 and is then trained end-to-end on nine datasets with wide-FoV augmentation, whereas VGGT and π3 appear to be evaluated off the shelf on distorted inputs for which they were not designed. There is no π3 baseline retrained on the same data, no equal-data replacement of the point head, and no practical cubemap/rectification baseline. Consequently, the dramatic gains cannot be attributed specifically to the angular/radial representation or camera token.

The key ray formulation is insufficiently specified and partly circular as written. Equation 8 evaluates spherical harmonics at angles θ and φ even though those angles appear to be the quantities that must be inferred from pixels. It is unclear whether coefficients are global, per-token, or per-pixel, how normalized 3D rays are obtained, what harmonic order L is used, and exactly where and how the camera token is injected. The Angular Module, Radial Module, and pose head are not described at an implementable level.

Important spherical-geometry details are omitted. The angular L1 loss in Eq. 9 does not discuss azimuth wrap-around or polar singularities, both central for full-sphere imagery, and the equation inconsistently uses ω and ω* in its condition. The treatment of normals and convolutions across the equirectangular seam is also unspecified.

The reconstruction protocol is unusually permissive: predictions are sequentially aligned with Umeyama, MoGe optimal point alignment, and ICP. The paper does not explain which degrees of freedom each stage removes, whether parameters and correspondence rules are identical for every method, or how much performance changes without ICP. This makes it difficult to determine how much of the reported result reflects globally consistent feed-forward reconstruction rather than post-hoc fitting.

Evaluation breadth is offset by limited statistical rigor. Stanford2D3D pose evaluation contains only 20 sampled cases from two subareas, FIORD uses only three scenes, and no confidence intervals or variation over sampling seeds are reported. Metric units and several protocol details, including scale handling for ATE/RPE, are missing. The Matterport localization study covers only three scenes and is not consistently superior to IM360 in pose AUC despite wording suggesting superior accuracy overall.

The ablations are incomplete and occasionally overinterpreted. There is no direct ablation of the spherical-harmonic ray head, angular/radial decomposition, π3 initialization, augmentation, or loss terms. Mixed-camera training is not uniformly better across all reported metrics—for example, adding all camera types can worsen completion relative to some subsets—yet the text states broadly that it improves performance.

Reproducibility is currently poor: the paper omits training duration/iterations, batch construction and dataset mixing ratios, dataset sample counts and exact splits, SH degree, module dimensions, token parameterization, exponential-decay rate, λ_trans, Huber threshold, inference memory, and parameter count. No code or model-release statement is provided.

Originality is moderate rather than high because the principal components closely follow π3's local permutation-equivariant reconstruction, UniK3D's spherical-harmonic ray representation and asymmetric loss, and prior calibration-token conditioning. The manuscript needs stronger controlled evidence that their combination yields benefits beyond appropriate wide-FoV training of the existing backbone.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical gap: feed-forward multi-view reconstruction for fisheye and panoramic imagery, where pinhole-oriented models often fail.
The ray-direction/radial-distance decomposition is geometrically sensible, and combining it with camera-type conditioning provides a plausible way to share a model across projection families.

Evaluation covers several outputs—pose, point maps, localization, and panoramic depth—on multiple fisheye and 360-degree datasets. The reported improvements over directly applying VGGT and π3 are large, especially on Stanford2D3D.

The Matterport3D localization experiment indicates a potentially valuable speed/coverage tradeoff: complete registration in seconds, albeit with lower accuracy than the strongest SfM pipeline on some scenes.
The manuscript is generally organized and includes a useful, though limited, discussion of dynamic scenes as a limitation.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the originality is limited. The method largely combines π3's permutation-equivariant reconstruction, UniK3D's spherical-harmonic ray representation, and camera/calibration-token ideas already discussed in prior work. The paper does not establish that their integration requires a substantial new technical insight.

The experimental comparison is not controlled. VGGT and π3 are applied to distorted images despite being trained for perspective imagery, whereas Wid3R is trained on nine datasets with explicit fisheye/360-degree supervision and augmentation. Comparisons against equally trained or fine-tuned baselines, rectification-based versions, and a π3 model with a conventional point head are necessary to attribute gains to the proposed representation rather than training-data advantage.

The central architectural claims are inadequately ablated. There is no direct-point-head versus angular/radial-head comparison, no ablation of spherical-harmonic degree or ray loss, and no isolation of pretraining effects. The camera-token ablation shows only modest changes in one setting and lacks repeated-run uncertainty or significance analysis.

The method is materially underspecified. The manuscript omits the spherical-harmonic degree, precise coefficient parameterization, token dimensionality and injection mechanism, head architectures, training duration, batch construction, dataset mixing ratios and sizes, and several optimization details. Equation 8 also writes the ray coefficients as depending only on the camera token, leaving their dependence on image features or pixel position unclear. Equation 9 contains inconsistent starred/unstarred angular variables and does not clearly define its thresholding operation.

The claim of handling diverse camera models without calibration is insufficiently demonstrated. Conditioning uses only three coarse camera categories, although cameras within a category have varying intrinsics and distortion parameters. There is no calibration/ray-direction evaluation, sensitivity test to an incorrect token, test on unseen camera models or distortion parameters, or analysis of how per-camera calibration is recovered from appearance alone.

The evaluation protocol can conceal reconstruction errors. Point clouds undergo Umeyama alignment, MoGe optimal alignment, and ICP in sequence, but the fitting scope, degrees of freedom, and whether exactly identical processing is applied to every baseline are not specified. Such strong ground-truth-assisted alignment can obscure scale and pose failures.

Several evaluations are too small or selectively reported for the breadth of the claims: Stanford2D3D pose uses only 20 sampled cases, large-scale localization uses three Matterport3D scenes, and no confidence intervals or variation over random samples are given. There is also no standard pinhole benchmark showing that the unified model retains competitive performance on its third claimed camera category.

The panoramic-depth comparison is difficult to interpret because Wid3R's training collection explicitly includes Matterport3D, yet Table 6 places it among foundation-model methods with an unspecified training-to-test source. The evaluation also does not clearly state whether predictions receive scale or shift alignment. Consequently, the apparent comparison to zero-shot or directly supervised methods is not transparent.

Some claims overstate the evidence. The abstract's improvement of '+77.33' is not tied to a named metric there, 'consistently outperforms' overlooks the lower AUC than IM360 on two of three localization scenes, and the conclusion claims superior monocular depth despite Wid3R having substantially worse AbsRel than the supervised methods and Depth Anywhere.

Overall, the practical direction and reported results are promising, but missing controlled baselines, incomplete ablations, ambiguous equations, and insufficient reproducibility prevent a convincing scientific case in the current form.

strengths: Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution because no type is explicitly declared. The paper addresses an important and underexplored computer-vision problem: feed-forward multi-view reconstruction directly from fisheye and 360-degree imagery, without rectification or explicit calibration.

The combination of ray-direction/radial-distance prediction, spherical-harmonic ray encoding, and camera-model conditioning is technically sensible. Although the ingredients build on UniK3D, camera-token adaptation, and π3, integrating them into a unified multi-view reconstruction system is useful and practically significant.

The empirical results are strong across several tasks and datasets. Wid3R substantially improves pose estimation over VGGT and π3 on FIORD, Zip-NeRF, and especially Stanford2D3D; it also produces large improvements in point-map accuracy, completion, and normal consistency on ScanNet++, Matterport3D, and Stanford2D3D.

The evaluation is broader than a single benchmark: it covers camera pose, dense reconstruction, large-scale localization, and monocular panoramic depth. The approximately three-second Matterport3D runtime, compared with minutes for optimization-based systems, demonstrates a meaningful efficiency advantage.

The paper is generally clear and well organized, with an intuitive architecture diagram, useful qualitative comparisons, explicit training losses, diverse real and synthetic training data, and a relevant discussion of the limited availability of 360-degree supervision.
weaknesses: The novelty is partly compositional: the permutation-equivariant backbone and much of the pose machinery come from π3, while the spherical-harmonic ray representation follows UniK3D and camera tokens have close precedent in fisheye depth adaptation. The paper's main novelty is therefore the multi-view integration and empirical validation rather than a fundamentally new geometric formulation.

The ablations do not sufficiently isolate the central architectural claims. Table 7 studies the camera token, data composition, and number of frames, but does not ablate the angular/radial decomposition, spherical-harmonic representation or degree, asymmetric ray loss, camera augmentation, or initialization from π3. In addition, the claim that mixing all camera types consistently improves 360-degree geometry is stronger than the table supports: compared with sphere-only training, the all-camera setting improves completion and variance but slightly worsens mean accuracy and normal consistency.

Baseline coverage leaves an important fairness question. VGGT and π3 are evaluated directly on distorted imagery for which they were not designed; comparisons against practical rectification, cubemap/perspective projection, or per-view camera-agnostic geometry followed by pose estimation would clarify how much of the gain comes from avoiding an intentionally mismatched input representation.

Several implementation and formulation details are missing or ambiguous, limiting reproducibility: training iterations, batch composition, dataset sampling ratios, spherical-harmonic order, precise camera-token insertion, parameter count, and memory cost are not reported. Equation 9 also contains inconsistent notation involving omega and omega-star, and the normalization of some losses is unclear.

Some evaluation choices need stronger justification. Point maps are subjected to a sequence of Umeyama alignment, MoGe optimal alignment, and ICP, which may conceal global or scale errors unless identical settings and pre-alignment results are documented. Statistical uncertainty is generally absent, Stanford2D3D pose evaluation uses only 20 sampled cases, and the large-scale localization study covers only three scenes with mixed accuracy relative to IM360.

The claims around monocular depth and generality should be moderated. In Table 6, Wid3R has excellent delta-1 accuracy but substantially worse AbsRel than several specialized and foundation-model baselines. The approach also requires a known discrete camera-category token and is not tested on unseen projection models, inaccurate tokens, non-central cameras, or continuous distortion variations. The limitations section mentions dynamic scenes but omits these more immediate constraints and provides no failure-case analysis.

strengths: Addresses an important practical gap: feed-forward multi-view reconstruction directly from fisheye and equirectangular imagery, without requiring rectification at inference time.

The combination of per-view local geometry, ray/radial decomposition, spherical-harmonic ray prediction, and camera-type conditioning is technically plausible and well motivated for wide-field-of-view cameras.

Evaluation covers several relevant tasks and datasets, including pose estimation, point-map reconstruction, monocular panoramic depth, and large-scale localization. Gains over the original VGGT and π3 models are especially large on 360-degree imagery.

The adapted π3 baseline trained on the authors' wide-angle data is valuable: it shows that training-data composition explains a substantial portion of the improvement while the proposed representation provides additional gains, particularly for point-map quality.

The method has clear potential impact for robotics, mapping, and AR/VR. The reported approximately three-second large-scene inference time is attractive compared with optimization-based spherical SfM pipelines.
The paper is generally clear, visually polished, and accompanied by useful qualitative results and a candid limitation concerning dynamic scenes.
weaknesses: The central architectural novelty is moderate because the method largely combines π3's multi-view backbone and local-coordinate formulation with UniK3D-style angular/radial heads and spherical harmonics. The camera token is the clearest new element, but its implementation and empirical isolation are insufficiently detailed.

The main comparisons confound architecture with substantially different training data. The authors' π3 retraining helps, but a complete factorial ablation is missing: ray representation without camera tokens, tokens without ray decomposition, matched parameter counts, and identical training schedules are needed to establish which component causes the gains.

The camera-token ablation is limited to Stanford2D3D, apparently only two scenes and 20 sampled cases, with no multi-seed training results or significance analysis. Its improvement is modest on some metrics, while the reported sample-level standard deviations are large.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important information such as spherical-harmonic order, exact token insertion mechanism and dimensions, module architectures, optimization duration, batch composition, learning-rate decay parameters, parameter count, computational cost, and dataset split construction is absent or underspecified.

Point-map evaluation applies Umeyama alignment, an additional optimal point alignment, and ICP sequentially. This permissive post-alignment may hide global pose, scale, or deformation errors; results before ICP and a precise description of the degrees of freedom fitted by every stage are needed.

Some empirical claims are overstated. In monocular depth, Wid3R has strong delta-threshold accuracy but substantially worse AbsRel than leading Matterport3D-specific methods. In large-scale localization it registers all views quickly but trails IM360 on several AUC results, and the study covers only three scenes.

The claimed calibration-free generality is not fully demonstrated. Conditioning uses only three discrete camera-family tokens, while real cameras vary continuously in intrinsics and distortion parameters. There is no held-out-camera-model or unseen-lens experiment showing generalization within or beyond these categories.

The pose results reveal tradeoffs that receive little discussion: on FIORD, Wid3R is worse than the data-matched π3 baseline in RTA, AUC, ATE, and translational RPE. More analysis is needed to explain when ray decomposition helps or harms.

The paper calls several evaluations 'zero-shot' even though ScanNet++, Matterport3D, and other dataset families are also used for training. Even if official scenes are disjoint, the terminology and exact train/test separation should be clarified, with explicit leakage checks.

The supplementary panorama-generation discussion is speculative and provides no integrated experiment. It should not be presented as evidence of applicability without measuring whether Wid3R actually improves generative consistency.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical gap: feed-forward multi-view reconstruction from fisheye and 360-degree imagery without an explicit image-undistortion stage. This is relevant to robotics, mapping, and AR/VR.

Combining per-view local reconstruction with angular/radial ray prediction is technically sensible. The method is evaluated on pose estimation, point-map reconstruction, localization, and monocular panoramic depth across several camera types.

The reported gains over the original VGGT and π3 models are large, especially on Stanford2D3D and Zip-NeRF. The comparison with a π3 model retrained on the authors' wide-angle data is particularly useful because it partially separates architectural improvements from training-data effects.
Qualitative results generally support improved reconstruction completeness, and the system is substantially faster than the optimization-based pipelines in the Matterport3D localization experiment.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the architectural originality is limited. The method largely combines π3's permutation-equivariant multi-view framework with UniK3D's spherical-harmonic ray decomposition, while camera/calibration tokens have also appeared previously. The paper's main novelty is therefore the integration and application to multi-view wide-FoV reconstruction, rather than a fundamentally new formulation.

The central 'first' and state-of-the-art claims are insufficiently established. Recent universal reconstruction systems such as MapAnything and Depth Anything 3 are cited as using ray representations but are not experimentally compared, nor is their inability to process the evaluated camera settings demonstrated. The cubemap alternative is addressed only through one qualitative example, without quantitative accuracy, memory, or runtime comparisons.

The evaluation does not cleanly isolate the proposed components. Retraining π3 on the authors' large composed dataset accounts for much of the improvement over published baselines. Wid3R improves further on most tests, but is worse than retrained π3 on FIORD pose AUC. There is no controlled ablation separating the angular/radial representation, spherical harmonics, radial self-attention, camera tokens, and camera-specific augmentation.

Point-map evaluation applies Umeyama alignment, an additional optimal point alignment, and ICP in sequence. This unusually strong test-time alignment can conceal scale, pose, or global-consistency errors central to the reconstruction claims. The paper does not justify this protocol, quantify each alignment's effect, or report results before ICP.

Several evaluation sets are very small: Stanford2D3D uses two scenes and only 20 resampled cases, FIORD uses three scenes, and Zip-NeRF uses four. No confidence intervals, per-scene results, or sensitivity to random sampling are reported, making the very large improvements difficult to assess statistically.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Important details are missing, including the spherical-harmonic order, camera-token dimensions and exact insertion points, λ_trans, training duration/iterations, batch composition, dataset mixing probabilities, invalid-pixel handling, and inference use of predicted uncertainty. The displayed project-page link is empty, and no code or trained models are provided.

The technical presentation leaves ambiguities. Equation 8 does not clearly specify whether coefficients are global or spatially varying or how image coordinates map to its angular variables for arbitrary projections. Loss normalization and masking are inconsistent or unspecified, and numerical handling of arccos-based rotation and normal losses is omitted.

The evidence does not fully support several broad claims. The model still requires the camera category token to be supplied at inference, robustness to unknown or continuously varying lens models is not tested, and calibration or projection-parameter perturbations are absent. Dynamic scenes are mentioned, but other important limitations—camera-model misclassification, seams and poles in equirectangular images, cross-device generalization, and compute/training cost—are not analyzed.

Some reporting is misleading or inconsistent: the abstract mixes absolute percentage-point gains with relative percentage improvements, and the claim of superior large-scale localization is overstated because Wid3R is worse than IM360 on two of the three Matterport3D scenes despite being much faster. Overall, the idea is useful and results are promising, but missing contemporary comparisons, an overly permissive alignment protocol, limited controlled ablations, and incomplete reproducibility leave consequential doubts about the scientific case.

strengths: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the paper addresses an important and under-served computer-vision problem: feed-forward multi-view reconstruction directly from fisheye and 360-degree imagery without image rectification or camera-specific preprocessing.

The combination of per-view local geometry, spherical-harmonic ray prediction, radial-distance estimation, and camera-model conditioning is technically sensible. Although it builds substantially on UniK3D and pi3, extending these ideas into a unified multi-view wide-FoV system is a meaningful contribution.

The empirical improvements are large and consistent across several tasks and camera regimes. Wid3R substantially improves pose estimation over VGGT and pi3, including AUC@30 of 74.61 on Zip-NeRF and 79.93 on Stanford2D3D, and produces markedly better point-map accuracy, completion, and normal consistency.

Evaluation is unusually broad, covering fisheye and spherical imagery, pose estimation, point-map reconstruction, monocular panoramic depth, and large-scale localization. The datasets include both indoor and outdoor scenes and both synthetic and real imagery.

The comparison against pi3 trained with the authors' wide-angle data is valuable: it shows that data composition accounts for part of the gain, while Wid3R's representation provides substantial additional improvements, particularly on Matterport3D and Stanford2D3D.

The method registers every image in the three reported large-scale Matterport3D scenes in approximately three seconds. While it does not always match the strongest optimization-based system's pose AUC, the accuracy-efficiency tradeoff is compelling.

Ablations support the usefulness of the camera token, mixed-camera training, larger multi-view batches, and the selected attention design. The finding that pinhole and fisheye supervision improves held-out 360-degree reconstruction is practically interesting.
The manuscript is clearly organized, visually polished, and generally easy to follow; the qualitative reconstructions strongly agree with the quantitative trends.
weaknesses: The architectural originality is moderate rather than fundamental: the angular/radial spherical-harmonic formulation closely follows UniK3D, while the multi-view backbone and local-coordinate formulation derive from pi3. Camera or calibration tokens also have close precedent. The paper's strongest contribution is therefore the integration and validation for wide-FoV multi-view reconstruction, not wholly new individual components.

The central controlled comparison is only a wide-angle-trained pi3 model. Comparable fine-tuning of other strong multi-view baselines, especially VGGT, is absent, so the results do not fully separate architectural advantages from training-data and optimization advantages.

The ablation does not isolate the angular/radial ray representation independently from all associated architectural and loss changes. A full factorial comparison of point-map versus ray output, with versus without camera tokens under identical training, would make the causal case substantially stronger.

The claimed camera-model generality is tested using three coarse, known categories—pinhole, fisheye, and spherical—and inference requires selection of the appropriate token. Generalization to unseen projection functions, lenses or intrinsics, mixed cameras within a sequence, and an unknown or incorrect camera token is not evaluated.

Some evaluations are limited in scale: Stanford2D3D pose testing uses only 20 sampled cases, and large-scale localization covers three Matterport3D scenes. Confidence intervals or repeated-run variability are not reported for the main comparisons.

The point-map protocol applies Umeyama alignment, an additional optimal point alignment, and ICP sequentially. The manuscript should justify this strong post-alignment pipeline, specify it completely, and confirm that it is identically applicable to every baseline, since it can conceal global pose and scale errors.

The monocular-depth claim is somewhat overstated. Wid3R has excellent delta-1.25 and competitive RMSE, but its AbsRel of 0.227 is worse than most specialized Matterport3D methods; the result is promising but not uniformly state of the art.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete, including training duration or iteration count, batch configuration and sampling probabilities, learning-rate decay parameters, spherical-harmonic degree, parameter count, memory scaling, and precise runtime hardware/protocol. No concrete code or model-release commitment is stated.

The method description contains technical ambiguities: the angular loss notation in Eq. 9 appears inconsistent about the target angle, spherical azimuth wrap-around is not discussed, and the exact pathway by which the camera token conditions all prediction heads is insufficiently specified.

The limitations discussion only mentions dynamic scenes. It should also address dependence on labeled geometry and pose across numerous datasets, the required camera-category token, robustness to unusual or imperfect camera models, computational scaling with view count, and failure cases under weak overlap or severe occlusion.
